newsitem.title: USA: NYC Hevesi says sports added $7 bln to '95 economy.
newsitem.headline: NYC Hevesi says sports added $7 bln to '95 economy.

text.p: New York City Comptroller Alan Hevesi said Wednesday the sports industry contributed $6.9 billion to the city's $302 billion economy in 1995, which made it about equal in size to the construction industry.
The estimate was broken down between about $3.8 billion of activity that sports added directly, with the rest flowing from indirect benefits.
Marketing produced an estimated $1.6 billion, sports publishing was worth around $1.5 billion, and television network fees were about $975 million, including both direct and indirect benefits.
As an example, Hevesi noted the magazine Sports Illustrated, located in New York City, which had $600 million of revenues in 1995.

The comptroller noted that of all the nine major league professional teams, the Yankees were worth the most, as they produced an estimated $307 million in 1995, followed by the Mets at $211 million, the Knicks at $196 million, and the Rangers at $156 million.
The report also found that Yankee Stadium cost the city government about $1.1 million a year, while the city makes about $700,000 a year from Shea Stadium, where the Mets play.
Horseracing adds about $345 million to the city's economy, with other professional sports, soccer, golf and bowling generating about $190 million.
The U.S. Open tennis matches contributed a total of about $226 million, more than any professional team other than the Yankees.
Hevesi also highlighted the substantial indirect benefits. "While the players provide excitement, it's the advertisers, broadcasters, writers and lawyers who score the most for our economy."
He estimated New York has about 450 lawyers with sports-related clients, from whom they earn an average of $80,000 a year.
